text: Last lesson built a real MERGE INTO upsert for the Silver layer, matched on transaction_id instead of a full nightly rewrite. Now let's stress-test that design against something every real retail pipeline eventually hits: data that arrives a day later than it should. Here's a concrete scenario, and a careful walk through why this pipeline handles it correctly without any special-case code anywhere.

Picture a customer buying something in-store on June first, late at night, right as that store's point-of-sale terminal starts losing its connection. Because of that sync delay, the sale doesn't make it into June first's export file at all. Instead it shows up bundled into June second's file, a full day later than it actually happened. This is completely normal, real-world behavior for any retail system — networks drop, terminals batch their uploads, and stores close before a sync finishes.

Walk it through layer by layer, starting with Bronze. Incremental ingestion reads whatever new file physically landed today, June second, and appends every single row inside it, sale_date column and all — it doesn't know or care that one of those rows actually happened yesterday. So the late sale lands in Bronze today, still carrying its real, original sale_date of June first, completely untouched.

This is exactly where last lesson's design choice pays off. The MERGE INTO matches incoming rows by transaction_id, never by when they happened to be ingested. This particular sale's transaction_id has never been seen before, so it hits WHEN NOT MATCHED and gets inserted — with sale_date still correctly reading June first. Nothing anywhere in this statement ever touches or overwrites that date column.

Both Gold tables aggregate GROUP BY sale_date, never by the date a row happened to load. So the very next Gold refresh folds this transaction into June first's totals, right where it honestly belongs — even though it physically arrived in the pipeline on June second. Contrast that with a naive design that stamped every row with today's date, or matched the MERGE on sale_date instead of transaction_id: either mistake would quietly inflate June second's numbers and under-count June first's.

No backfill job, no manual correction, and no late-arrival special case anywhere in this pipeline — incremental ingestion simply preserves the real date it already had, and a transaction_id-keyed MERGE doesn't care when a row happened to show up. Next lesson, you'll build the Regional Manager's brand-new Gold table on top of this now-correct, now-trustworthy Silver layer.
